That a promissory note is treated like land. The Sema holds, as he explains at length in the Derishah, that even if the debtor never had land and presently has none, a debt evidenced by a promissory note is nevertheless considered a claim secured by land merely because a lien on land is mentioned in the note. The Taz follows him. Their proof is from the Tur, who cites Tosafot and the Rosh as saying that according to the view that a lien on property is of Torah origin, one cannot find a Torah oath in a case of partial admission and the like except where the debtor has no land. They infer that a note must be treated as a land secured obligation even where the debtor has no land. If the debtor actually had land, then even an oral loan or a handwritten acknowledgment would also be secured by land. The distinction must therefore be that a formal promissory note itself is treated as a land secured claim even where there is no land. The Shach disagrees, and the Bach appears to agree with him. In their view, if the debtor has no land, even a promissory note has no land lien and cannot be called a land secured claim. The reason a promissory note is sometimes called a land secured obligation, while an oral loan and handwritten acknowledgment are not, is that the creditor may waive his right against the debtor personally without waiving his right against encumbered property. It is for that reason that the formal note is described as secured by land. It is true that Tosafot at the beginning of Bava Metzia, in the sugya of heilech, write a distinction of this kind. Yet it is difficult to fit into the Tur's language. The Tur should not have stated without qualification that a promissory note is a land secured obligation. He should have specified the circumstances described by the Shach, where the creditor waived recourse against the debtor personally but not against encumbered property. There is another difficulty. The Tur first cites Ramban's position that if the note was lost or cannot be authenticated, it is not considered a land secured claim. The Tur then writes: but Tosafot and the Rosh say that partial admission requiring a Torah oath can be found only where the debtor has no land, etc. This clearly indicates that Tosafot and the Rosh disagree with Ramban. According to the Shach, however, Ramban could fully agree with their statement. Ramban may simply be speaking about the kind of note described by the Shach, where the creditor waived recourse against the debtor personally but retained recourse against encumbered property. So long as the note exists and is enforceable, he can collect from purchasers and it is therefore a land secured claim. If the note is lost or cannot be authenticated, he can no longer collect from purchasers and it is no longer a land secured claim. There would be no dispute at all. It therefore appears that the Derishah was troubled by Tosafot in Shevuot. Regarding Rabbi Yochanan's statement that one who denies a loan supported by witnesses is liable for a false oath offering, whereas one who denies a loan evidenced by a promissory note is exempt because it is a claim secured by land, Tosafot and the Rosh ask that Rabbi Yochanan holds that liens are of Torah origin. If so, even a loan supported by witnesses should be a claim secured by land. Tosafot answer that the debtor has no land, or that the creditor waived the land lien. The question still remains: if the debtor has no land, then the loan evidenced by a promissory note should likewise not be land secured. Tosafot in Bava Metzia themselves notice this and answer, as the Shach does, that the creditor may have waived recourse against the debtor personally without waiving recourse against encumbered property. But in Shevuot they do not raise or answer this second question. Maharam of Lublin already expresses astonishment at this in his novellae to Bava Metzia. The Derishah sought to prove from the omission that Tosafot there hold that even without existing land, a formal promissory note itself is considered land secured. In truth, the Shach is correct that such a proposition has no sound basis. The difficulty in Tosafot and the Rosh can be resolved easily. They may hold, like most authorities, that after the Sages enacted that an oral loan cannot be collected from purchasers, there is no operative lien at all upon the borrower's land as against purchasers. At every moment the borrower may sell his land without the creditor being able to prevent it. The fact that the creditor can collect from land that remains in the borrower's possession does not reflect a continuing property lien. It is merely the general rule that collection from the debtor himself may be made even from the cloak on his back. Thus an oral loan no longer has the status of a land secured obligation. Tosafot's question there, however, concerns the Torah's original law. The Torah imposes an oath in a case of partial admission. According to the view that liens are of Torah origin, an ordinary debt under Torah law would be secured by land. Where, then, is the Torah oath of partial admission found? Tosafot answer that under the Torah law one finds such an oath where the debtor has no land or where the creditor waived the land lien. Rabbi Yochanan's statement, by contrast, concerns practical halachah after the Sages enacted that an oral loan does not collect from purchasers and thereby removed its land lien. Therefore, even where the debtor owns land, one who falsely denies an oral loan supported by witnesses can be liable for the oath offering because the debt is no longer treated as a land secured claim. A formal promissory note is different. Its lien against purchasers remains in force because the Sages did not remove it. Everything is thus properly explained. This, in my view, is clearly the Tur's understanding. For this reason, throughout siman 75 and siman 87, where the Tur discusses the rules of Torah oaths and the distinctions between Torah and rabbinic oaths, he never states that the borrower must specifically be a person who owns no land or that the creditor must have waived the lien. As practical halachah, no such condition exists. Even where the borrower owns land, the Sages removed the purchaser lien from an oral loan. This applies to an oral loan or handwritten acknowledgment. A formal promissory note, however, retains its land lien when the debtor has land. This is the actual distinction between a formal note and an oral or handwritten debt. The Tur cites Tosafot and the Rosh to establish precisely this conceptual point. The Ran in Shevuot, whose words I discussed at length above in siman 75, answers the original difficulty differently. What does it matter that the debtor's property is legally subject to the debt? If the creditor later seeks to collect from purchasers, the purchasers will deny the debtor's admission and say, "What does your admission matter to us? You are speaking falsely. You never borrowed, or you already paid." Accordingly, the admitted portion is not practically collectible from purchasers and should not be considered an admission concerning land, even if the Torah recognizes a general land lien. Ramban too accepts this answer, as the Rosh cites in his name at the end of chapter Shevuat HaPikadon. Tosafot and especially the Rosh there reject this answer. They hold that once the underlying obligation is one for which land is legally encumbered, it is treated as a land secured claim even if, in practice, the creditor cannot collect from purchasers because they will not accept the debtor's admission. Therefore, under Torah law, an ordinary loan secured by land does not generate a Torah oath of partial admission, and we must establish the Torah's oath in a case where the debtor has no land. The practical difference between these approaches emerges with a formal promissory note whose purchaser lien normally remains intact but which has been lost, while the debtor admits that it existed. According to Ramban, the debt is no longer a land secured claim because the creditor cannot collect from purchasers. They are entitled to reject the debtor's admission and say that perhaps there never was a note or perhaps the debt was repaid. The debtor's partial admission can therefore generate a Torah oath. According to Tosafot and the Rosh, however, the underlying debt is of a type that carried a land lien from its inception. The inability to collect from purchasers because the note was lost does not change the nature of the debt. This is exactly like the Torah law of partial admission discussed above, where the purchaser may not practically believe the debtor but the claim is still characterized as land secured because of the underlying lien. Thus, even when the note has been lost or cannot be authenticated, if the debtor admits its existence, no Torah oath of partial admission arises. This is clear and correct. See the Rosh at the end of chapter Shevuat HaPikadon and his words will explicitly support this explanation. The same is evident in chapter 2 of Ketubot. The Rosh discusses a husband who says, "I married you as a widow and your ketubah is one hundred," while the woman says, "I was a virgin and my ketubah is two hundred." He explains that the husband does not take a Torah oath as one who partially admits because the ketubah is a land secured obligation. The Rosh cites the Yerushalmi concerning a note stating unspecified sela'im where part of the writing was erased. The creditor says the amount was five and the debtor says it was three. Ben Azzai says that since the debtor partially admits the claim he must swear. The Sages say that this is not an admission of the same kind as the claim. The Rosh explains that the admission concerns land. Although the remaining text of the note itself proves only two sela'im, once the debtor admits a third, it is treated as though the third had also been written into the note. The denial concerns movable money while the admission concerns a land secured debt. The Yerushalmi then asks from the ketubah case. There, seemingly, the husband's admission is of the same kind as the woman's claim. She no longer holds a note in her hand. She says two hundred and he says one hundred. The Yerushalmi answers that everyone agrees she is entitled to one hundred, meaning that he cannot deny that basic amount. Therefore, it is treated as though she has a note for that one hundred, and that portion is land secured. At first glance this passage is very difficult. How can the Rosh cite the Yerushalmi when it appears to contradict the Bavli in Bava Metzia? In the Bavli's case of a note saying merely "sela'im," where the debtor admits three, the third sela is not treated as a land secured obligation. The Gemara explicitly distinguishes the first two sela'im, which are evidenced by the note, from the third, which exists only by the debtor's oral admission. There is another difficulty. The Mishnah concerning the ketubah applies both in a place where ketubot are ordinarily written and in a place where they are not, as is clear from Ketubot 16b, where Rabbi Elazar establishes the Mishnah in a place where ketubot are written and derives from it that a receipt may be written. In a place where ketubot are written, if the woman does not present her ketubah, the Rosh follows the Rif that Rabbi Yochanan's rule that one cannot plead payment against an obligation imposed by beit din does not apply. The husband can claim that he paid. How then can the Yerushalmi say that he cannot deny the first one hundred and that it is treated as though a note exists? According to what I have written, everything is correct. The baraita cited in the Bavli concerns a note that originally stated only the unspecified word "sela'im." An unspecified plural means two. No formal note ever existed for the third sela. Thus, when the debtor admits a third, that third amount is only an oral admission. There never was a land lien evidenced by the note for it. The Yerushalmi, however, speaks of a note that contained an amount which was later erased. If the note originally stated three, then the third sela was originally secured by the written note exactly like the first two. The fact that the writing is now erased and purchasers will not accept the debtor's admission does not matter according to the Rosh's view. The underlying third sela was originally a land secured debt. It is therefore treated as an admission concerning land, just as I explained above regarding a lost or unauthenticated note. The same applies to the ketubah in a place where ketubot are ordinarily written. Originally, when the ketubah existed, the basic one hundred was land secured. Even though the woman now cannot collect from purchasers because she lacks the document and they may claim it was paid, the underlying obligation was originally secured. According to the Rosh, that is sufficient to characterize the husband's admission as concerning land. Why then does the Yerushalmi emphasize that the husband cannot deny the basic one hundred? Because the Mishnah also applies in a place where no ketubah document is ordinarily written. In such a place, if the husband could plead payment, there may never have been any written instrument or enduring land lien at all. The obligation could resemble an oral debt whose purchaser lien was removed. Therefore the Yerushalmi explains that everyone agrees the woman is entitled to the basic one hundred. In a place where no writing is customary, the obligation created by beit din itself gives her an unavoidable basic claim. But in a place where ketubot are written, once the obligation was originally secured, it makes no difference that he may now plead payment. The Rosh's words are thus entirely clear. The Rosh does not explain the Sages in the Yerushalmi the way the Bavli explains its own baraita, namely that the first two sela'im are a land secured admission and therefore, had the debtor merely admitted two, there would be no oath, while an admission of three still leaves him as one who voluntarily returns a lost item because he could have admitted only the two already stated in the note. The Raah explains along those lines. The Rosh does not, because in the Yerushalmi case the note originally contained more and was later erased. There is no written support for the proposition that only two were owed. Thus the debtor is not like one voluntarily returning a lost item by admitting the third. In the Bavli's case, by contrast, the note itself says merely "sela'im," which ordinarily means two. That writing supports the debtor's claim that no more than two were owed. He could therefore be viewed as voluntarily admitting the third, and Tosafot explicitly use the fact that the note supports him to explain why he is considered one returning a lost item even though ordinarily one who partially admits has a migo to deny everything. The note's text gives him unusual boldness to deny beyond the two because it supports his position. In the Yerushalmi, where the original amount was written and later erased, there is no such support from the document. The debtor cannot be considered one returning a lost item merely because he admits three. The Rosh therefore explains the Sages' exemption by saying that the third sela itself is treated as a land secured admission. Everything fits precisely. From this Yerushalmi the Rosh could indeed derive his rule that where a debt was originally secured by a note, the loss or erasure of the note does not remove its characterization as a land secured obligation for purposes of a Torah oath. One may ask according to this approach from the Gemara's question against the opinion that heilech exempts: why did Scripture need a special exclusion to exempt land from an oath? Even if heilech generally exempts, the exclusion for land should still be necessary in a case of partial admission where land was originally encumbered but later sold, according to Tosafot and the Rosh. Purchasers will not accept the debtor's admission, so the creditor cannot actually collect even a needle's worth of land from them. The admission would therefore not be heilech. Yet according to the Rosh it remains a land secured admission because the original lien existed. Tosafot themselves explain that when the Gemara asks why a verse is needed to exclude land, the question is not literally whether the Torah could have used the verse for some other law. The question is why the Mishnah needed to teach the land exclusion as an independent application. By the era of the Mishnah, the Sages had already removed the purchaser lien from oral loans. Thus the ordinary cases before the Mishnah would not involve a surviving land lien on an oral partial admission. This removes much of the difficulty. Still, one can ask from a formal promissory note that was later lost. According to the Rosh and Tosafot, if the debtor admits the debt it remains a land secured claim, but because the note is lost the creditor cannot collect from purchasers who reject the admission. It is therefore not heilech. Why then was the Mishnah's exclusion of land not needed for precisely such a case? We must say that the proposition that a formal note is a land secured claim is itself accepted even according to the opinion that liens are not of Torah origin. The Gemara routinely treats a formal promissory note as land secured without making that characterization depend upon the Torah origin of liens. Even if liens are not of Torah origin, the Sages established a purchaser lien for formal notes, and actual land becomes legally subject to the debt. But this is so only when the note exists and is enforceable. If the note is no longer present and only the debtor admits that it once existed, according to the opinion that liens are not of Torah origin there is no original Torah lien to preserve. The rabbinic lien was enacted only so long as the creditor possesses the enforceable note. Once the note is lost, the very rabbinic framework that created the purchaser lien no longer applies. The Sages said that he may collect from purchasers when the note is in his hand, and they equally determined that the lien is not enforceable when it is not. The Rosh and those who agree with him say that a lost note remains a land secured claim only according to the view that liens are of Torah origin. Under that view, the underlying debt carried a Torah lien from the outset. Although the Sages removed the lien from oral loans, they left the Torah lien intact in the case of a formal promissory note. The loss of the document may prevent practical collection from purchasers, but it does not change the original Torah character of the debt. According to the view that liens are not of Torah origin, however, once the rabbinic purchaser lien becomes unenforceable because the note is absent, no land secured status remains. The Gemara's question concerning heilech can therefore be understood according to the opinion that liens are not of Torah origin. Indeed, the sugya concerning an exchange indicates that Rav and Shmuel hold that heilech exempts, and they also hold that liens are not of Torah origin. Under their view, there is no case of a lost note that simultaneously remains a land secured claim and yet fails to be heilech. If the note exists, the claim is land secured and collection can proceed against the encumbered property. If the note is lost, the rabbinic lien itself no longer gives the claim land secured status. The Gemara's question is therefore properly framed. This also provides one way to answer a point I raised above at the beginning of siman 75. Tosafot there ask from Rabbi Yochanan's statement in Shevuot rather than asking internally from the baraita itself why there should be any difference between the first two sela'im stated in the note and the third sela admitted orally. One may say that the baraita's tanna could hold that liens are not of Torah origin, as I wrote above in siman 39 regarding Rabbi Meir. The first two are nevertheless secured because they are in the formal note, while the third admitted orally is not. Tosafot therefore challenge from Rabbi Yochanan, who himself holds that liens are of Torah origin. This is straightforward, although, as I wrote above, the matter may still be somewhat strained.
If he cannot establish it, the Mechaber states the law without qualification in accordance with the Ramban. As I wrote in the preceding seif katan, Tosafot and the Rosh disagree, for in any event there was a lien upon land, and it makes no difference that the purchasers would not believe him. I likewise found in the Asufot Zekenim to Bava Metzia, in the name of one of the great authorities, an explanation of the statement, “But the document that he admits to is heilech,” as referring to an uncertified document, so that his admission is required. According to that authority, the explanation must be as follows. One might ask why the Gemara assumes that the baraita concerns an uncertified document. The Gemara holds that something which cannot be denied is not considered an admission at all. If so, how could Rabbi Meir say concerning one who says, “three,” that he is returning a lost object because he has a migo that he could have denied everything? His admission to two would not be an admission in the legal sense at all. Therefore the Gemara establishes the case as one of an uncertified document. Then he is indeed returning a lost object, because even the two are within the category of an admission, since he could have denied them by claiming that the document was forged. The Gemara then asks why, regarding the two themselves, he should be exempt from an oath. If the reason is that he could have claimed forgery, then he has a migo that he could have denied everything. Rather, once he admits to the document, it is heilech. The Gemara answers that he is exempt either because the document supports him or because it is a claim involving a lien on land. Even though he could have claimed forgery, now that he admits the document it is nevertheless a land lien, as Tosafot and the Rosh wrote. This also resolves the question raised by all the commentators, namely, what did the questioner initially think? Did he not know that one does not take an oath concerning denial of a land lien? According to this explanation, it is clear. The questioner thought that since the document was uncertified and was established only through the borrower’s own admission, it was not a land lien, which is in fact the view of the Ramban. The Gemara answers that it nevertheless is a land lien, in accordance with Tosafot and the Rosh. This also resolves another difficulty. According to the initial assumption, before the Gemara knew that it was a land lien and exempted the defendant only because of heilech, why did it seek support from the baraita rather than from the Mishnah at the beginning of the second chapter of Ketubot, as the Rosh asks? There too the husband should have been obligated to take a Torah oath as one who admits part of the claim, and necessarily he is exempt because of heilech. Likewise, according to the answer that the document supports him, without relying either on heilech or on a land lien, the Mishnah in Ketubot remains difficult. There the document cannot be said to support the husband, because the woman’s ketubah does not itself establish whether she is entitled to one hundred or two hundred. According to what was explained, however, there is no difficulty. With a certified document the Gemara already knew that there is a land lien, and there the obligation is certified because a woman has a ketubah by stipulation and by act of beit din. Only here did the Gemara initially assume that the case concerns an uncertified document, because it had not yet introduced the rationale that the document itself supports him. We, however, rule that even with a certified document he is considered one who returns a lost object, because the Gemara introduced the additional rationale that the document supports him, and in every form of the case he is therefore returning a lost object, as Tosafot wrote. The inference is thus sound. If so, the great authority cited above likewise follows the approach of Tosafot and the Rosh. Perhaps that authority held like Tosafot in the chapter Eizehu Neshekh, that where the borrower himself does not claim forgery, beit din does not make a forgery claim for the purchasers and we do not suspect collusion. In that case it is indeed a land lien. According to the Ramban, however, and as I explained at length below in siman 106, we nevertheless make the forgery claim on behalf of the purchasers. If so, there would no longer be any lien upon land. This is somewhat strained, however, because it would mean that the questioner and the answerer in the Gemara disagree on that separate rule. However, however the matter is understood, Tosafot and the Rosh certainly disagree with the Ramban. I am nevertheless surprised that the Tur cites the words of Tosafot and the Rosh as practical law. The Rosh wrote at the beginning of the second chapter of Ketubot, as cited above, that the husband does not swear because his admission concerns a lien upon land. He then wrote that even after the enactment that a woman may collect from movable property, since one who makes a claim contrary to an act of beit din accomplishes nothing, this is heilech because he cannot deny the obligation. The Rosh thus taught that after the enactment of the Geonim a document is no longer called a land lien, and the exemption from a Torah oath rests instead upon heilech. Accordingly, where a document was lost and the debtor can deny the obligation, there is neither a land lien nor heilech, since he can deny it. The Maggid Mishneh likewise writes in chapter 17 of Hilkhot Ishut concerning the Rambam’s ruling where she says, “I was a virgin,” and he says, “you were a widow,” that the husband must take a Torah oath as one who admits part of the claim. The Raavad objects that this is a lien upon land. The Maggid Mishneh explains that the Rambam holds that after the enactment of the Geonim permitting collection from movable property there is no longer a land lien. He adds, however, that ordinarily the husband still cannot deny the obligation because one who contests an act of beit din is not believed. He therefore concludes that in a place where ketubot are written, if the ketubah was lost and the husband is believed to say that he paid it, he can deny the obligation, and because the enactment of the Geonim allows collection from movable property he is obligated in a Torah oath. See there. It is explicit from his words that without the Geonic enactment, even though the husband could claim payment, it would nevertheless be a land lien. This is precisely what I wrote concerning the Rosh and Tosafot. Yet after the Geonic enactment it is no longer a land lien. If so, according to our law the ruling concerning a document that was lost has fallen away entirely, because nowadays movable property may be collected under the Geonic enactment. It is true that in Even HaEzer siman 96 the Tur cites the Rosh’s view concerning the case where he says that she was a widow and she says that she was a virgin, ruling that in every place, even where ketubot are written, the husband takes only a heset oath. There too he is believed to claim payment and the principle concerning one who contests an act of beit din does not apply. The later authorities have already addressed this and explained that the Tur is speaking of a case where the husband had warned her not to accept payment except before witnesses, so that he can no longer deny even in a place where ketubot are written. But here the difficulty remains. One might answer, though with difficulty, that the Lechem Mishneh already asked why the Geonic enactment should matter at all. Any ordinary creditor may collect movable property under Talmudic law, and nevertheless a debt evidenced by a document is called a land lien. We must say that although the creditor may collect movable property as a matter of Talmudic law, movable property is not subject to a Torah lien. The Sages merely empowered him to collect movable property and descend to the debtor’s assets, while by Torah law collection is only from land, as the commentators wrote. Therefore a document is called a land lien even though movable property may also be collected, because the essential lien rests upon land. A ketubah may be different. Since the Geonim enacted collection from movable property, and according to the Rosh the enactment has a root and basis in Talmudic law, such as the case of the camels of Arabia from which a woman collects her ketubah, the obligation is not exclusively a lien upon land. If one were to say that the primary Torah lien is nevertheless upon land, that applies to ordinary creditors. A ketubah itself is rabbinic, and the Sages who created it also defined its mode of collection. There would therefore be no stronger reason to characterize the land than the movable property as the principal lien. Still, this distinction is strained. Regarding the Lechem Mishneh’s underlying question, it seems that when an ordinary creditor collects movable property, it is not because the movable property itself is encumbered. If it were, he should also collect it from orphans, just as when a person expressly designates his ox as an apotiki, thereby expressly encumbering movable property, the creditor may collect it from the heirs, as the Rashba writes. Rather, movable property is not subject to the lien at all. The debtor himself is liable even from the garment upon his shoulders because repayment of a debt is a mitzvah, but the orphans are not personally obligated in that mitzvah. Consequently, movable property is not part of the lien. Even when the creditor presents his document, his secured claim is only against land, not against movable property, and it is not a claim that combines land and utensils. By contrast, under the enactment of the Geonim, which permits collection even from the movable property of orphans, it is clear that they instituted an actual lien, as though the debtor had written that movable property would be encumbered to the creditor without attaching it to land. Such movable property is encumbered and may be collected from heirs, although not from purchasers because it lacks publicity, as the Rashba writes. Once movable property enters the lien in the same manner as land, a claim upon the document becomes like a claim upon land and utensils together. The Lechem Mishneh’s difficulty is therefore resolved on its own. Nevertheless, it appears that even apart from this, the later authorities already noted a difficulty in the Tur’s unqualified ruling that even in a place where ketubot are written, if the ketubah is not in her possession, the husband takes only a heset oath. The explanation that the Tur is speaking of a case where he warned her not to accept payment except before witnesses is strained, as is evident there. It may therefore be that the Tur was troubled by the Lechem Mishneh’s question: what practical difference is created by the Geonic enactment if every creditor already collects movable property? He did not accept the distinction offered above. He therefore understood the Rosh differently. The Mishnah teaches that where witnesses exist the husband is believed, which implies that without witnesses he is believed without a Torah oath because the admission concerns a land lien. One might ask how the Mishnah can state the rule without qualification. Granted, where he owns land, but where he owns no land what can be said? There the husband should have to take an oath. The answer is that if he owns no land the ketubah cannot be collected at all, because originally a ketubah was collected only from land. If he does own land, it is again a land lien. The difficulty is only with the Rif, who reproduces the ruling without qualification that the husband is believed. After the Geonim enacted collection from movable property, there is now a practical case where the husband owns no land yet the ketubah may still be collected. The Rosh therefore explains that even then he cannot deny, because a claim contrary to an act of beit din is ineffective. Alternatively, the Rosh intended to teach an independent law, that even if the husband has no land he does not swear. This is the meaning of his statement that “even after the enactment of the Geonim” the result is unchanged. There now exists a case where he owns no land, yet there is still no oath because he cannot deny the obligation. Accordingly, all the words of the Rosh apply where the debtor has no land. Where he does have land, the fact that movable property may also be collected does not remove the status of the claim as a land lien. Therefore the Tur, who speaks in the ordinary case where the debtor has land, as I explained in the preceding seif katan and as the Shach also wrote, rules here that the document remains a land lien. So too in Even HaEzer the Tur speaks ordinarily of a husband who owns land. It therefore always remains a land lien even though collection is also possible from movable property. This is why the Tur rules that the husband is obligated only in a heset oath. Similarly, in his Kitzur Piskei HaRosh he writes that where a ketubah was lost, namely in a place where ketubot are written, the husband takes only a heset oath, and he does not say that the law changed after the enactment. This understanding resolves the difficulty. Furthermore, a clearer and more correct explanation follows from what I write below in siman 107 in resolving the apparent contradiction in the words of the Tur and the Rosh. In one place they write that the Geonic enactment was not merely an enactment but follows from the underlying law, as above, because movable property is like the camels of Arabia. Elsewhere they write that it is not the underlying law but only an enactment. There I explained that in damages and similar obligations, where the creditor had no opportunity to stipulate and write security terms, we say that collection from movable property is rooted in the law itself. But where a document is written, it cannot be said that the parties relied upon movable property. Had they intended that, the document should have expressly mentioned both movable property and land. See there at length. Accordingly, the Rosh may hold that where reliance upon movable property and collection from it exist by the underlying law, a document is no longer called a land lien, because movable property too is truly encumbered. The claim is then like one who claims utensils and land and the defendant admits part of both, which produces a Torah oath. But where movable property is not collectible by the underlying law, and the parties did not rely upon it, and collection exists only because of the enactment, the original lien evidenced by the document never loses its character as a land lien. The Rosh’s words are therefore precise. When he writes that even after the Geonim a woman collects from movable property, he is not speaking of a place where ketubot are written. In such a place the parties could have written the security expressly, and thus collection from movable property is not by the underlying law. His question concerns a place where ketubot are not written, where the case is truly comparable to the camels of Arabia and movable property is legally encumbered. In that setting he answers that the husband cannot deny the obligation, because Rabbi Yochanan said that one who contests an act of beit din accomplishes nothing. The Rosh’s rulings thus apply in all circumstances. In a place where ketubot are written, the Geonic enactment does not alter the character of the original lien. In a place where they are not written, the husband cannot deny the obligation. Therefore the Tur rules without qualification, both in his Kitzur Piskei HaRosh and in the Tur itself, that there is never a Torah oath, for one of these two reasons always applies. It follows that the Tur acted correctly in not stating here that after the Geonic enactment, where a document was lost and the debtor can deny the obligation, it ceases to be a land lien. With an ordinary written loan, the rule resembles a place where documents are written. Movable property of heirs is collected only because of the enactment, not under the underlying law, as the Tur himself writes in siman 107. Therefore the document remains a land lien. The same is true even if we adopt only the explanation of the Sema and the Shach that Tosafot and the Rosh hold that even nowadays an admission of part of a documented claim is a land lien where the debtor owns land. If this were not so, the Geonic enactment itself would determine the law and there would be no land lien. Examine this carefully. This, however, is the view of the Tur and the Rosh. The Maggid Mishneh understands the Rambam differently. According to him, even in a place where documents are written, once the document is lost and the debtor can deny the obligation, after the Geonic enactment there is no longer a land lien. The Shulchan Aruch in Even HaEzer siman 96 cites both opinions, the Rambam’s view and the Rosh’s view, whereas here the Mechaber rules without qualification like the Rambam. This is thus a case of an anonymous ruling followed elsewhere by a dispute. It also appears from the foregoing that where we say that if the debtor owns no land even a document is not considered a land lien, there is a question regarding land that he acquired later, where the document did not expressly include a clause encumbering property to be acquired in the future. Is that later acquired land enough to characterize the claim as a land lien? It seems that this depends upon a dispute. According to the Ramban, if the borrower dies the creditor cannot collect such property from the heirs at all, only from the borrower himself. If so, there is no true lien upon that property, and the case resembles movable property under the Talmudic rule governing ordinary creditors. Since the property never entered the lien, the claim cannot be treated as one upon both land and movable property. According to those who disagree with the Ramban and hold that even from heirs such later acquired property may be collected, it resembles movable property after the enactment of the Geonim. Although the creditor cannot collect it from purchasers, it nevertheless forms part of the lien, and the claim is therefore treated as one involving land.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
ושל השטר שכפר וכו' ואע"פ שיש לו מגו דהיה כופר בהך דבע"פ והיה מודה בהך דבשטר ואף נגד שטר אמרינן מגו כדקי"ל בהמפקיד בשטר דנאמן לומר החזרתי במגו דנאנסו דשם יש לו מגו בגוף שטר ואיתרע שטר אבל כאן אין לו מגו בגוף שטר ושטר בחזקתו ש"ך ועיין לעיל בכללי מגו דאם ל"א מגו מממון לממון בלא"ה לק"מ ע"ש:
דשטר הוי כמו קרקע פי' הסמ"ע אפילו לית ליה קרקע כלל מ"מ הואיל ושטר ה"ל ש"ק אם יש לו קרקע מיקרי שעבוד קרקעות. והש"ך השיג עליו ועיין תומים שהארכתי והעליתי דבעינן דוקא דאית ליה קרקע הן ב"ח והן משועבדים אבל בלית ליה קרקע לא הוי ש"ק ואפשר אפילו יש לו קרקע והוא דאקני ובשטר לא שיעבד דאקני ג"כ לא ה"ל ש"ק דהא יכול למוכרו ואין מוציא מיד לקוחות ולא משתעבד כלל ומ"מ צ"ע ועיין תומים:
על כפירת וכו' דכמו דאין נשבעין על קרקע והתורה ממעטינהו משבועה כן בשטר שיש בו שעבוד על קרקע ה"ל כקרקע גופיה והא דדרשינן גם כן דשטרות אין נשבעין אין פירושו הך דינא דזהו בכלל קרקע רק פי' דתבעו דמסר לו ב' שטרות בעין והוא מודה לו בא' סמ"ע ופשוט:
כהודאה ע"פ כתב הסמ"ע בטור הביא דעת התו' והרא"ש דאפי' במ"מ גרידא ליכא שבועה למ"ד שעבודא דאורייתא אלא בדלית לי' קרקע והמחבר והרב השמיטו. ועיין תומים דכתבתי דליכא למ"ד הכי כלל רק כי פליגי בהיה לו שטר ואינו מקוים או נאבד והוא מודה בו בהא נחלקו דהם סבירא להו דמ"מ הוי שעבוד קרקעות ע"ש שהארכתי בזה וכתבתי אף על גב דמחבר סתם פה דלא ה"ל ש"ק וחייב ש"ד בא"ע סימן צ"ו סעיף ט"ו הביא מחלוקת בזה:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
And the portion in the document that he denied, etc. Although he has a migo that he could have denied the oral claim and admitted the portion evidenced by the document, and we do sometimes accept a migo even against a document, as in the case where one is believed to say, 'I returned it,' through a migo of unavoidable accident, there the migo attacks the document itself and thereby weakens it. Here he has no migo concerning the document itself, and the document remains in its original force. Shach. See the general rules of migo. If one does not employ a migo from one monetary matter to another, the issue is simpler still.
A document is like land. Sema explains that even if the debtor presently owns no land, the written obligation is treated as a land-secured claim because if he did own land the document would create a lien on it. Shach objects. See Tumim, where I discussed this at length and concluded that actual land is required, whether unencumbered or already sold. If he owns no land, the claim is not treated as land-secured. It is possible that even if he owns land acquired only later, but the deed did not include an after-acquired-property clause, the claim is not treated as land-secured, because he may sell that land and purchasers cannot be foreclosed upon. This remains unresolved. See Tumim.
On the other hand, and so on, Do not swear on the ground and the Torah from its smallness, it is not the case that Hashem is working on the ground of his body, nor does he mention that he is not in the eye, nor does he admit to him that he does not mean that he is not the same as Hashem’s judgment in the eye, and he is grateful to him
Like an oral admission. Sema writes that Tur cites Tosafot and Rosh as holding that even an ordinary partial admission does not generate an oath according to the view that property liens are Torah law, unless the debtor owns no land. Mechaber and Rama omitted this. See Tumim. I wrote that no authority actually holds that in the broad form stated. The real dispute concerns where there had been a document that is not authenticated, or was lost, and the debtor admits it. Some authorities treat even that as a land-secured obligation. See there. Although Mechaber rules here that it is not land-secured and therefore a Torah oath applies, in Even HaEzer 96:15 he brings a dispute concerning this issue.

mechaber.he: בד"א בשטר שטורפים בו מהמשועבדים אבל כתב ידו אפי' יש בו נאמנות כיון שאינו טורף בו ממשועבדים דינו שחייב שבועה דאורייתא כמו במלוה על פה:
mechaber.en: This rule applies to a written document through which one may collect from encumbered property. An obligation in the debtor's own handwriting, however, even if it contains a trustworthiness clause, does not permit collection from encumbered property and therefore has the same law as an oral loan: the defendant is obligated in a Torah oath.

baer_hetev.he: נאמנות. והש"ך כתב דדין זה צ"ע דנרא' דעת הרמב"ם ושאר פוסקים דבכת"י בנאמנות הוי הילך וטעמא לפי שאינו יכול לכפור גם בא"ע סימן צ"ו סט"ו כתב הרמ"א בהג"ה דבדבר שא"י לכפור לא הוי מודה מקצת אפי' ליכא שעבוד קרקעות ע"ש (ובספרי מ"ז בא"ע שם ביררתי דזה אינו דמה שכ' הרמ"ה שם דנשבע היסת הוא מטעם דבמקום שאין כותבין כתוב' הוי כתוב' שעבוד קרקעות ע"ש) וכן משמע בתשובת מבי"ט ח"ב ס"ס ר"ה וא"כ נראה פשוט לענין דינא דאין לחייבו ש"ד דלא יהא אלא ספיקא דדינא הוי קולא לנתבע עכ"ל:
baer_hetev.en: Credibility. The Shach writes that this ruling requires study. It appears that the Rambam and other authorities hold that a handwritten acknowledgment containing a credibility clause is considered "here it is," because the debtor cannot deny it. In Even HaEzer siman 96, seif 15, the Rama likewise writes that regarding a matter the defendant cannot deny, there is no partial admission even where there is no lien upon land. See there. In my work on Even HaEzer there I established that this proof is not correct. The Ramah's statement there that the defendant takes a hesset oath is because in a place where people do not ordinarily write a ketubah, the ketubah itself is treated as a claim secured by land. See there. The same implication appears in Responsa Mabit, part 2, at the end of siman 205. It therefore appears straightforward as a matter of practical law that we should not obligate him in a Torah oath. At the very least this is a case of legal doubt, in which the defendant receives the benefit of the doubt. Shach.

beer_hagolah.he: שם ס"מ כ"כ בה"ת בשער ז' וכתב והכי הסכימו רבוותא קמאי ז"ל וכ"כ ה"ה שם בפ"ר בשם הרמב"ן
beer_hagolah.en: There, seif 40. So writes Baal HaTerumot, gate 7, adding that the early great authorities agreed. The Maggid Mishneh likewise writes in the name of the Ramban.

beur_hagra.he: בד"א כו'. כיון שאינו גובה ממשועבדים שלכן אמרו שעבוד קרקעות ואע"ג שא"י לכפור שיש בו נאמנות וה"ל לפטר מטעם הילך כמ"ש שם בגמ' הילך ג"כ דוקא בשעבוד קרקעות כמ"ש רש"י שם ד"ה טעמא כו' וכל משמעות השטר כו' שהרי הקרקעות כו' והשיב הגמ' א"נ כו' דבלאו הילך נמי דה"ל שטר כו' ולכן לא נקיט הרי"ף טעמא דהילך דהילך נמי משום שיעבוד קרקעות וכן טעמא דמסייע לא שייך אלא בסלעים דינרין שתובעו מחמת השטר וכן לא שייך טעמא דירושלמי כל עמא מודי כו' דדוקא בכתובה דהטוען אחר מעשה ב"ד כו' וכמש"ל סי' ע"ה ס"ב ושכן מוכח מירושלמי וז"ש רמב"ם בפ"ג מה' טוען ונטען אין מודה כו' עד שיודה בדבר שאפשר לכפור כו' שהשטר לא כו' והרי כל נכסיו משועבדים כו' דוקא משום שנכסיו משועבדים ולכן כ' בפט"ז מה' אישות הל' כ"ה ואם היה הבעל קיים כו' ודברי המ"מ שם צ"ע שכ' שאין נק' שיעבוד קרקעות אא"כ אינו גובה אלא מקרקעות וא"כ במלוה נעולם יהא חייב ואף שם השיגו הראב"ד כיון שהוא מקום שאין כתובה ה"ל שיעבוד קרקעות וע"ש ובש"ע א"ע סי' צ"ו ובפכ"ב מה' עדות הל' ב' יראה לי כו' וע"ש בהשגות ובכ"מ בשם הר"ן שכ' כיון דא"א לכפור ה"ל שיעבוד קרקעות ור"ל כיון שהוא שטר וגובה ממשועבדים וכדיירי רש"י אבל הרמב"ם שם הולך בשיטת רבו שכ' בעה"ת בשכ"ט ח"ג ויש לנו לברר זה שאמרנו לענין מלוה אחד ולוה אחד וב' שטרות כו' וזה שאנו אומרים כו' ע"ז כ' הר' אבן מגש כו' ממשועבדים אין מן הדין לגבות בשטרות כאלו לפי שכל שטר מהן יש לנו לומר שמא זה השטר פסול הוא ואין גובין בו הלכך אע"פ כו' ע"ש וזה טעם הרמב"ם שנשבע ש"ד:
beur_hagra.en: When does this apply, etc. Because the debt is not collectible from encumbered property, the reason of land lien does not apply. Although the debtor cannot deny the debt because the instrument contains a clause of trust, one cannot exempt him merely through the rule of ‘here it is.’ In the Gemara that rule itself is tied specifically to a lien upon land, as Rashi explains: the entire force of the document lies in the land. The Gemara then gives another answer, that even without ‘here it is’ he is exempt because the claim is supported by a document. Rif therefore does not cite the reason of ‘here it is,’ since that reason too depends upon the land lien. The argument that the document assists him applies only where the claimant’s demand arises from the document itself, such as sela'im or dinars. The Yerushalmi’s rule that everyone agrees in the ketubah case likewise applies specifically to an obligation created by an act of beit din, as explained above in siman 75. Thus, where there is no collection from encumbered property, the exemption does not follow automatically.

ketzot_hachoshen.he: כת"י ומדין אינו יכול לכפור עמ"ש בסי' פ"ז סק"ה:
ketzot_hachoshen.en: His handwriting, and legally he cannot deny it. See what I wrote in siman 87, seif katan 5.

meirat_einayim.he: אפי' יש בו נאמנות. זהו דלא כמ"ש המ"מ בפירושו להרמב"ם איך שס"ל דאם יש בו נאמנות לא מחשבא הודא' דהרי בלא הודאתו נמי הי' חייב ובאידך ה"ל כופר הכל ועד"ר:
meirat_einayim.en: Even if it contains a credibility clause. This is unlike the Maggid Mishneh's explanation of Rambam, according to which a credibility clause would prevent the admission from being treated as a partial admission because the debtor would already be obligated without his admission, leaving the other portion as a complete denial. The present ruling rejects that understanding. See the Perishah.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: יש בו נאמנות. והש"ך חולק כיון דמודה במה שא"י לכפור הוי הילך:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: It contains a credibility clause. The Shach disagrees. Since he admits only something he could not have denied, it is treated as "here it is."

pitchei_teshuva.he: יש בו נאמנות. עבה"ט ועיין בתשו' עבוה"ג ס"ס קי"ג מ"ש בזה:
pitchei_teshuva.en: He has loyalty. A thick hull and a humming with a thick hull and a snail in this:

siftei_kohen.he:
אפי' יש בו נאמנות כו'. ולפע"ד דין זה צ"ע לפי שנרא' שפסק המחבר כן ע"פ מ"ש בספרו ב"ה דאפשר גם הרמב"ם סובר כן ובאמת נלפע"ד דעת הרמב"ם דבכתב יד בנאמנות הוי הילך דכתב טעמא לפי שאינו יכול לכפור וכ"כ ה' המגיד והנ"י רפ"ק דמציעא בשמו (ודלא כב"ה לדעת הרמב"ם) וכ"כ בס' לח"מ פ"ד מה"ט בדעת הרמב"ם אך מה שהקש' שם הלח"מ על הנ"י שלא הבין דעת הרמב"ם כן הוא תמוה לי שאדרב' הנ"י כתב כדבריו שוב ראיתי בכסף משנה פ' כ"ב מה' עדות דעתו גם כן דדעת הרמב"ם כמו שכתבתי ע"ש והבאתי דבריו לעיל סימן ל"א ס"ב גם ר' ירוחם כתב כן במסקנתו בנ"ג ח"ב וז"ל ויש מי שכ' שכל זמן שהודה בדבר שלא הי' יכול לכפור כמו בכת"י בנאמנות ה"ל הילך ופטור מש"ד וכ"כ הרמב"ם ז"ל עכ"ל וכ"כ עוד ר' ירוחם שם בסתם בסוף החלק ההוא ע"ש וכ"כ הרא"ש רפ"ב דכתובות דבדבר שא"י לכפור ה"ל הילך ומביאו ב"י לעיל ר"ס פ"ז וכן דעת ה' המגיד פ"ה מה' טוען דלא כמו שנרשם כאן בגליון סמ"ע ע"ש ה' המגיד להפך וע"ל סימן פ"ז ס"א בהג"ה משמע ג"כ הכי והוא מהטור ע"ש ודוק וכ"כ בסמ"ג דף קפ"א ע"ג להדיא דשטר הוי הילך שהרי לא תועיל בו כפירתו ולא הזכיר שום שעבוד קרקעות ע"ש וכ"כ בס' מעד"מ בריש ב"מ שדעת הרא"ש והרמב"ם דכל שא"י לכפור ואפי' אינו שטר לא הוי מ"מ וכ"כ הב"ח שכן דעת הרמב"ם והרא"ש והטור ע"ש:
שוב ראיתי בא"ע סימן צ"ו סט"ו מביא הר"ב גופיה דעת ה' המגיד פ' ט"ז מה' אישות דס"ל דבדבר שא"י לכפור לא הוי מ"מ אפי' ליכא שעבוד קרקעות ואזיל לטעמי' בפ"ד מה' טוען ומביאו ב"י שם ע"ש וכן משמע בתשו' מבי"ט ח"ב ס"ס ר"ה ואם כן נרא' פשוט לענין דינא דאין לחייבו ש"ד דלא יהא אלא ספיקא דדינא הוי קולא לנתבע:
siftei_kohen.en: Even if it contains a clause of credibility, etc. In my humble opinion this ruling requires study. It appears that the Mechaber ruled this way based on what he wrote in Bedek HaBayis, that perhaps the Rambam also agrees. In truth, however, it appears to me that the Rambam holds that a handwritten obligation containing a credibility clause is heilech, because the Rambam explains the reason as being that the defendant cannot deny it. The Maggid Mishneh and Nimukei Yosef at the beginning of Bava Metzia also explain the Rambam this way, contrary to Bedek HaBayis's understanding. Lechem Mishneh, chapter 4 of Hilchos To'en, likewise understands the Rambam this way. His challenge there to the Nimukei Yosef, as though the Nimukei Yosef did not understand the Rambam that way, is puzzling, for the Nimukei Yosef actually writes exactly this. I later saw that the Kesef Mishneh in chapter 22 of Hilchos Edus likewise understands the Rambam as I have written, and I cited his words above in siman 31, seif 2. Rabbeinu Yeruham also reaches this conclusion in Nesiv 3, chelek 2, writing that some authorities hold that whenever one admits something he could not have denied, such as a handwritten obligation with a credibility clause, it is heilech and he is exempt from a Torah oath, and that the Rambam writes so. Rabbeinu Yeruham later states this ruling without qualification at the end of that section. The Rosh at the beginning of the second chapter of Kesubos likewise holds that something which the defendant cannot deny is heilech, as cited by the Beit Yosef above at the beginning of siman 87. The Maggid Mishneh in chapter 5 of Hilchos To'en holds the same, contrary to the marginal note here in the Sema that cites him for the opposite. See there. The gloss in siman 87, seif 1, likewise appears to rule this way, following the Tur. The Semag explicitly writes that a document is heilech because denial cannot avail against it, without mentioning any land lien. Maadanei Yom Tov at the beginning of Bava Metzia likewise writes that according to the Rosh and Rambam, whenever the defendant cannot deny the admitted portion it is not considered a partial admission, even without a formal document. The Bach also writes that this is the view of the Rambam, Rosh, and Tur. I later saw that in Even HaEzer, siman 96, seif 15, the Rama himself cites the Maggid Mishneh in chapter 16 of Hilchos Ishus as holding that where the defendant cannot deny a matter, it is not a partial admission even when there is no land lien, consistent with the Maggid Mishneh's approach in chapter 4 of Hilchos To'en, as cited by the Beit Yosef there. The responsa of Mabit, volume 2, end of siman 205, likewise appear to support this. Accordingly, the practical ruling is plainly that he cannot be obligated in a Torah oath. At the very least it is a matter of legal doubt, and in a doubt concerning an oath we rule leniently for the defendant.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he:
אפי' יש בו נאמנות כו' הש"ך השיג שדעת הרמב"ם והרא"ש דכל שאין יכול לכפור תו לא הוי הודאה לזקוק לשבועה ועי' מה שהאריך ותחילה נחקור בדברי רמב"ם דכתב בפ"ד מהל' טוען דהודה בחמשים בשטר לא מיקרי מ"מ שהרי שטר לא תועיל בו כפירתו והרי כל נכסיו משעובדים לו ואפילו היה כופר היה חייב לשלם וכו' עכ"ל ומזה למד דס"ל לרמב"ם כל שאין יכול לכפור לא הוי הודאה וכ"כ המ"מ בפט"ו מהלכות אישות במקום שאין כותבין כתובה דא"י לכפור לא הוי הודאה והביאו רמ"א א"ע סי' צ"ו סט"ו: ואני תמה א"כ למה כתב הרמב"ם הרי כל נכסיו משעובדי' לו מה צורך לזה הל"ל סתם דא"י לכפור והא לפ"ד אף בכת"י שיש בו נאמנות דעתו אמור' ובכת"י ליכא שעבוד אלא ברור דהא א"י לכפור לא הוי הודאה הוא מטעם הילך כמ"ש הרא"ש בפ"ב דכתובות ועכצ"ל כן דאל"כ מה טרח הגמרא שם ב"מ במלוה אומר שתים למה פטור משבועה ולא קאמר דא"י לכפור כקושי' הר"ן אלא דטעמו משום הילך דאם יכול לכפור אין זה הילך דממה יגבה הלא אם ימכור נכסיו יצחקו עליו הלקוח' ופקע שעבודו ושטר בלי דנשתעבדו קרקעות לא ה"ל הילך כמ"ש הע"ש דהרבה יש להם שטרות ואינם מקבלים פרעון עיין לעיל ריש פ"ז אלא עיקר הילך מחמת דנשתעבדו נכסים וה"ל כגבוי וכמ"ש רש"י וכמש"ל סי' פ"ז. וזהו אם אין יכול לכפור א"כ נשתעבדו נכסים וה"ל הילך אבל ביכול לכפור ולא נשתעבדו נכסים ויכול למוכרן א"כ לא ה"ל כגבוי ולא ה"ל הילך. ולכך כתב הרמב"ם דהרי לא תועיל בו כפירתו והרי כל נכסים משעובדים תרתי בעינן שעבוד נכסים ולא יועיל כפירתו ואז ה"ל הילך ולא קשה א"כ דל הילך מהכא הא ה"ל שעבוד קרקע ואין נשבעין וזהו היה כל הכרח שהכריח למחברי' דכוונתו של רמב"ם אפילו לכת"י בנאמנות. דזהו אינו דהרמב"ם כ' זה כן האידנא דתקנו גאונים לגבות מטלטלין דיתמי או דכ' בשטר מא"ק א"כ תו ליכא שעבוד קרקע כמ"ש הרא"ש והמ"מ דה"ל כתבעו בכלי' וקרקעות ולכך נתן טעם דמה בכך מ"מ אף קרקעות משעובדים לו ואם לא ימצא מטלטלין ע"כ יגבה מקרקע ה"ל הילך דהא א"א להמלט שלא יגבה חובו ודבריו ברורים ופשוטים וכמ"ש הרא"ש דאף דלבתר תקנת גאונים פקע שעבוד קרקע מ"מ הלך מיקרי. ויפה כתב המ"מ וכן הרמ"א בכתוב' במקום שא"כ הואיל ולא יכול לכפור לא מיקרי הודאה דשם נשתעבדו נכסים מטלטלין וקרקע וה"ל הילך כיון דאין יכול לכפור. ותמהני מהש"ך שהביא ראיה משם דבמקום דלא נשתעבדו נכסיו ה"ל הילך: ויש ראיה לזה בהא דכתב הרמב"ם בפ' ט' מהל' נ"מ בשני' רודפין אחד גדו' ואחד קטן כו' דכתב הרמב"ם דמיירי דיש עדים על הנגיחה רק לא ידעו מי נגח גדו' או קטן וכתב הרמב"ם בזה אומר גדול וזה אומר קטן או זה מועד וזה תם ישבע המזיק ש"ד דהודה במקצת והא בנגיחת הקטן והתם א"א לכפור דיש כאן עדים בנגיחה. ודוחק לומר כמש"ל דמיירי דהודה קודם שבאו עדים ואח"כ באו עדים וא"כ אז בעת הודאה יכול לכפור דזה דוחק דה"ל לרמב"ם לפרש זה דדוקא בכה"ג חייב שבועה ועוד א"כ אם יהיה מודה ואח"כ יהיה נמצא שטר יהיה נקרא יכול לכפור דסוף כל סוף ה"ל שטר או עדים ובפרט בהך דנגיחה דעיקר הודאה תלי' בעדים דאל"כ ה"ל מודה בקנס וה"ל טענו בחיטין וכו' וא"כ דעיקר הודאה תלי' בעדים והרי אינו יכול לכפור וזהו לענ"ד כמעט ראיה שאין עליו תשובה בכוונת הרמב"ם ז"ל. ואחרי אשר בררנו דעת הרמב"ם נשוב לדברי הרא"ש אן כוונתו נוטה כי הרב מעדני מלך ואחריו הש"ך תפסו דבריו במ"ש בפ"ב דכתובות לפי שאינו יכול לומר פרעתי כר"י הטוען אחר מעשה ב"ד וכו' הלכך האי מנה דמודה ביה ה"ל הילך כיון דאין לו טענה לפטור הימנו וכו'. דסתם בכ"מ דא"י לכפור ואפילו בכת"י דיש בו נאמנות ולענ"ד נראה דגם הוא דעתו כמ"ש ברמב"ם דמלבד דדוחק דבשביל שלא יכול לכפור יהיה נקרא הילך מה הילך הא יכול להבריח הכל ול"ל שעבוד כלל ומה ענין זה להילך והנ"י והר"ן דתפסו כוונת הרמב"ם דא"י לכפור לא דנו בו הטעם משום הילך רק ס"ל דלא הוי הודאה ועדיין העזה דרבה במקומו דמה שמודה הוא מוכרח אבל הרא"ש דכתב להדי' משום הילך ק' לומר בזה בכת"י דאין כאן שיעבוד כלל אף גם דהרא"ש סייע דבריו מדברי ירושלמי דכת' דלכך במשנה ליכא ש"ד דכ"ע מודה דחייב לה מנה ופי' הרא"ש דא"י לכפור דהטוען אמב"ד וכו' הלכך כאלו יש לה שטר על אותו מנה ושיעבוד קרקעות הוי וכו' הרי דדייק הרא"ש דש"ק הוי ולדבריהם מה צריך לש"ק הל"ל סתם א"י לכפור ואמת כבר עמד בזה הגאון מהורש"ק בתפארת שמואל וכ' לולי דכל גי' ספרים כך היה מוחק תיבת וש"ק הוי מדברי הרא"ש וח"ו דהא כל הנוסחא כך רק האמת דלולי דהוי ש"ק לא היה מועיל לא יוכל לכפור כלל דמ"מ לא הוי הילך דממה יגבה ולכך צריך תרתי ודבריו הן כדברי הרמב"ם הנ"ל דכלל תרווייהו כחדא א"י לכפור וש"ק ואמת כי דברי הרא"ש צריכין ביאור דמה סיוע מביא לדבריו מדברי ירושלמי דנשני' קודם תקנת גאונים וא"כ א"צ לטעם ודין של א"י לכפור רק דה"ל ש"ק וכמ"ש הרא"ש בעצמו במשנה לולי תקנת גאונים והא דכתב ירושלמי דא"י לכפור כבר בררתי לעיל דאל"כ במקום שאין כותבין לא הוי ש"ק כלל כמש"ל אבל מנ"ל הך דלאחר תקנה דליכא ש"ק דה"ל הילך מירושלמי הנ"ל ומה סיוע יש. ונ"ל דסבירא ליה להרא"ש הא דאמרינן כ"ע מודו אין הפי' הכל יודעין רק כ"ע בן עזאי וחכמים החולקים בשטר דכתב דאינון ונמחק דבן עזאי דמחייב שבועה בזו מודה ובן עזאי ע"כ סבירא ליה דנשבעין על הקרקעות דהיה מתחילה ש"ק בתוך השטר וכמש"ל באריכות וא"כ למה פטר במשנה וע"כ הטעם משום הילך אך זהו דוחק. דמילת כ"ע מודו פירושו הכל יודעים:
ולכן יותר נראה דקשיא ליה להרא"ש וכי לא ידע דכתובה ה"ל ש"ק דהא אין נגבית רק מן קרקע ואפילו במקום שאין כותבין ומה קשיא ליה לירושלמי ולכך נ"ל דבירושלמי שם פריך מה יהני עדים דלמא מ"ע היא ותי' חד תי' לא חשו לדבר דלא שכיח כלל וחד תי' דר"מ היא דסבירא ליה מ"ע גובה מאתים וס"ל להרא"ש כהר"ן ולא כר"ת דר"מ דסבירא ליה מטלטלין משתעבדי' לכתובה הוא אפילו מיתמי ואם כן קשה לר"מ ישבע דל"ל ש"ק דהא אף מטלטלין משתעבדי דמה שהוא לדידן לתקנת הגאונים הוא לר"מ מדין גמרא ועכצ"ל משום דא"י לכפור וה"ל הילך וא"ש ודוק מיהו צ"ע דבפרק האומר בקדושין כתב הרא"ש דאף לר"מ אין אשה גובה מיתמי ובהא לא פליג ר"מ מיהו שם הכל לישנא דתו' שהעתיק הרא"ש כנראה מלשונו שם ואפשר הוא לא סבירא ליה וצ"ע ועכ"פ הנכון בדברי הרא"ש כמ"ש דבעי ש"ק והוא דה"ל הילך ובחנם השיג המעדני מלך דטור סותר דעת הרא"ש. וכן מה שכתב הרא"ש בב"מ דשטר אין נשבע דה"ל הילך או משום דהוי ש"ק ומזה רצה לדייק דש"מ דהילך איירי בליכא ש"ק וזה אינו רק נ"מ לדידן לבתר תקנה או קודם תקנה בנכתב שטר מא"ק וזהו ודאי ליכא ש"ק רק הילך הוי ואחר שבררנו דעת הרמב"ם והרא"ש נשובה לחקור דעת שארי מחברים והנה רש"י כתב להדיא על האי שטר דקמוד' ביה הילך הוא כיון דמשועבד קרקע וכן כתב הג"ת והש"ך בס"ק מ"ז ביקש לדחות ראיה זו דרש"י לא אמרה אלא באין מודה בשטר ודבריו דחוקים דהא רש"י מפרשו על האי לישנא והאי שטר דקמודה ביה הילך היא וכיון דמודה ביה מה צורך לשעבוד קרקעות ואדרבא קשה על רש"י למה מחק גי' הישנה כיון דקמודה ביה משום דא"צ להודאתו אדרבא ה"ל לאוקמי דבס"ד דלא ס"ל דהוי שעבוד קרקעות היינו משום דהוי ס"ל דסתם שטר איירי אפילו בדלית ביה אחריות נכסים כדתנן בב"מ שטר שאין בו אחריות ולכך צריך לומר דקמודה ביה כמ"ש הש"ך דבשטר שאין בו ממשעבדי נקרא הילך כשמודה בו ולא כשהוא כופר ומה ראה רש"י למחוק גי' הישנה ועכצ"ל דס"ל לרש"י דבממ"נ אי ליכא שעבוד נכסים בכל אופן לאו הילך הוא כמש"ל מה הילך יש אם אין מקום לגבות וביש שעבוד נכסים א"צ להודאתו ולכך מחק רש"י וזה ראיה ברורה לדברי הג"ת. אך בזו יש לדחות רש"י לטעמי' דרש"י ס"ל דאפילו בהלואה ונותן המעות לא ה"ל הילך רק בפקדון וא"כ מה בכך דלא יכול לכפור וכי עדיף זה מאלו נותן המעות בב"ד ולכך הוצרך רש"י לומר דיש לו שיעבוד נכסים והוי כגבוי מאז ותמיד ברשותו קיימא כפקדון משא"כ לדידן דלא קימ"ל כרש"י א"כ י"ל כל שלא יכול לכפור ה"ל כהילך כאלו מוסר מעות בב"ד ובזה יש לדחות דברי הג"ת אך כ"ז דוחק ועיין באס"ז הרבה מחברים דכתבו דלא סגי במה שאין יכול לכפור עד שיהיה שיעבוד קרקעות נמי ולכן אין לזוז מדברי המחבר ולו נמטי אפריון:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en:
Even if it contains a clause of credibility, etc. The Shach objects that the Rambam and the Rosh hold that whenever a person cannot deny the obligation, his admission is not considered an admission that can generate an oath. See his lengthy discussion. We must first examine the Rambam’s words. In chapter 4 of Hilkhot To’en he writes that if one admits fifty by virtue of a document, this is not considered an admission of part of the claim, because his denial would not help against the document, all his property is encumbered to the creditor, and even if he denied the debt he would still have to pay. From this it has been inferred that the Rambam holds that whenever one cannot deny, his statement is not considered an admission. The Maggid Mishneh likewise writes in chapter 15 of Hilkhot Ishut that in a place where ketubot are not written, since the husband cannot deny the ketubah obligation, his statement is not considered an admission, and the Rama cites this in Even HaEzer siman 96, seif 15. I am surprised by this inference. If that were the entire reason, why did the Rambam add that all of the debtor’s property is encumbered? He should simply have written that denial is ineffective. According to the Shach’s understanding, the same law would apply even to a handwritten note containing a credibility clause, although such a note creates no lien upon property. Rather, it is clear that the inability to deny prevents the statement from being an admission because the admitted portion is heilech, as the Rosh wrote in the second chapter of Ketubot. This must be so. Otherwise, why did the Gemara in Bava Metzia labor to explain why, where the lender says that the loan was two and the borrower admits one, he is exempt from an oath? It could simply have said that he cannot deny the documented amount, as the Ran asks. The reason is that the exemption is heilech. If the debtor could deny the obligation, the admitted sum would not be heilech, because from what could the creditor certainly collect? If the debtor sold his property, the purchasers could dismiss the creditor and his lien would disappear. A document without an effective lien upon land is not heilech, as the Ir Shushan notes, since many people hold documents and nevertheless never receive payment. See above at the beginning of siman 87. The essence of heilech here is that the assets are encumbered and the sum is regarded as already collected, as Rashi writes and as I explained above in siman 87. Thus, where the debtor cannot deny, the assets are encumbered and the admitted amount is heilech. Where he can deny and there is no effective lien upon the assets, so that he can sell them, the debt is not regarded as already collected and there is no heilech. This is why the Rambam writes both that denial is ineffective and that all the debtor’s property is encumbered. Both elements are required: an effective lien upon the assets and the inability to deny. Only then is it heilech. One cannot object that if there is a land lien the defendant should in any event be exempt because one does not swear concerning land. This very point led the later authorities to think that the Rambam must be referring even to a handwritten note containing a credibility clause. But that conclusion is unnecessary. The Rambam wrote his ruling for the present law, after the Geonim enacted collection from the movable property of heirs, or for a document that expressly includes movable property together with land. In such cases the claim is no longer exclusively one involving a land lien, as the Rosh and Maggid Mishneh write, because it is like a claim upon both utensils and land. The Rambam therefore explains that even so, the admitted amount is heilech because the debtor’s land remains encumbered and, if movable property cannot be found, the creditor will necessarily collect from the land. The debtor cannot escape payment of the admitted amount. The Rambam’s words are therefore clear and straightforward, and accord with the Rosh, who writes that even after the Geonic enactment removed the exclusive status of a land lien, the admitted amount is nevertheless heilech. The Maggid Mishneh and the Rama also write correctly concerning a ketubah in a place where ketubot are not written. Since the husband cannot deny the obligation, and both movable and immovable property are subject to collection, the admitted amount is heilech. I am therefore surprised that the Shach cites that case as proof that even without any lien upon property the mere inability to deny creates heilech. There is a further proof from the Rambam’s ruling in chapter 9 of Hilkhot Nizkei Mamon. Where two animals pursued another animal, one large and one small, and witnesses saw the goring but did not know which animal caused it, the Rambam rules that if the injured party says the large animal gored and the owner says the small one gored, or one says the mu’ad animal caused it and the other says the tam caused it, the defendant takes a Torah oath because he admits part of the claim. Yet with respect to the goring by the small animal or the tam he cannot deny the event, because witnesses establish that some goring occurred. It is strained to say, as discussed above, that the Rambam refers only to a case where the owner admitted before the witnesses arrived, so that at the moment of admission he could still deny. Had this limitation been intended, the Rambam should have stated it. Moreover, according to such reasoning, whenever a person admits and a document is later discovered, his earlier admission would be treated as one made while denial was possible, even though the obligation is ultimately established by a document or by witnesses. This is especially difficult in the case of damages, where the legal force of the defendant’s statement itself depends upon the witnesses, for without them it could be an admission to a fine and would also raise the problem of claiming wheat and admitting barley. Thus the essential admission depends upon evidence that simultaneously prevents denial. In my view, this is nearly conclusive proof of the Rambam’s intent. Having clarified the Rambam, we return to the Rosh. The Ma’adanei Melekh, followed by the Shach, understood the Rosh’s statement in the second chapter of Ketubot, that because the husband cannot say “I paid” in the face of Rabbi Yochanan’s rule that one who contests an act of beit din accomplishes nothing, the one hundred that he admits is heilech because he has no defense against it, as a general principle that whenever denial is impossible, even with a handwritten note containing a credibility clause, there is no admission capable of generating an oath. In my view, the Rosh means the same as the Rambam. Quite apart from the difficulty of calling something heilech merely because denial is impossible, when the debtor may hide all his property and there is no lien at all, the Nimukei Yosef and the Ran, who understood the Rambam as teaching that inability to deny means there is no legally significant admission, did not explain the matter as heilech. Their rationale is that the admission lacks the element of brazenness described by Rabbah, because the defendant is compelled to concede that amount. The Rosh, however, expressly invokes heilech. It is difficult to apply heilech to a mere handwritten note where there is no lien upon any property. The Rosh also supports his words from the Yerushalmi, which says that the husband does not take a Torah oath because everyone agrees that he owes her one hundred. The Rosh explains that he cannot deny the obligation because of the rule concerning an act of beit din, and therefore it is as though she has a document for that one hundred and there is a lien upon land. The Rosh thus expressly emphasizes the land lien. According to the Shach’s approach, why is that needed? It would have been enough to say that the husband cannot deny. The gaon Rabbi Shmuel Kaidanover already noticed this in Tiferet Shmuel and wrote that, were the text not uniform in all manuscripts, he would delete the words referring to a land lien. Heaven forbid that such an emendation be made when all texts agree. The truth is that without a lien upon land, the inability to deny would not by itself create heilech, because there is no assured property from which collection may be made. Both elements are required, exactly as in the Rambam: he cannot deny, and there is a land lien. The Rosh’s use of the Yerushalmi still requires explanation. The Yerushalmi discusses the law before the Geonic enactment. At that time a ketubah was collectible only from land, so the exemption could simply rest upon the rule that one does not swear concerning land. Why does the Rosh need to derive from the Yerushalmi the later rule that after the enactment, when the claim is no longer exclusively a land claim, it is nevertheless heilech because denial is impossible? What support does the Yerushalmi provide for that later situation? One possibility is that the Rosh understood the Yerushalmi’s phrase “everyone agrees” as referring specifically to Ben Azzai and the Sages, who disagree where a document contained a sum and part of it was erased. Ben Azzai, who obligates an oath there, necessarily holds that an oath may apply despite the original land lien evidenced by the document, as explained above at length. If even Ben Azzai agrees that the husband is exempt in our Mishnah, the reason must be heilech rather than merely the land lien. This explanation, however, is strained, because the phrase “everyone agrees” ordinarily means that the matter is universally known, not that it refers to those particular disputants.
Therefore, it appears more likely that the Rosh was troubled by a different point. Surely the Yerushalmi knew that a ketubah is a claim involving land, since under the original law it was collected only from land, even in a place where no written ketubah was used. Why, then, did the Yerushalmi need another reason? In that sugya the Yerushalmi asks what help witnesses provide, since perhaps the woman is a woman who lost her virginity through an injury. One answer is that the Sages did not concern themselves with such an uncommon possibility. Another answer is that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that even such a woman receives two hundred. The Rosh may follow the Ran rather than Rabbenu Tam in understanding Rabbi Meir to hold that movable property is legally encumbered for a ketubah, even from orphans. If so, according to Rabbi Meir the husband should take an oath, because the claim is not exclusively a land lien. What for us is true only after the Geonic enactment was, according to Rabbi Meir, already true under Talmudic law. The Yerushalmi must therefore exempt him because he cannot deny the admitted amount and it is heilech. This provides the Rosh with a direct precedent for the post enactment law. Admittedly, in the chapter HaOmer in Kiddushin the Rosh writes that even according to Rabbi Meir a woman does not collect movable property from orphans, and Rabbi Meir does not disagree on that point. However, that passage appears to be copied from Tosafot, as its wording indicates, and perhaps the Rosh himself did not accept that detail. This requires study. In any event, the sound understanding of the Rosh is as stated: he requires both the inability to deny and an effective lien so that the admitted sum is heilech. The Ma’adanei Melekh therefore objected without basis that the Tur contradicts the Rosh. The same applies to the Rosh’s statement in Bava Metzia that one does not swear regarding a document either because it is heilech or because it is a land lien. The Shach wished to infer that the heilech rationale must refer to a case where there is no land lien. That is not necessary. The practical difference can be after the Geonic enactment, when movable property of heirs is collectible, or even before the enactment where the document expressly encumbers movable property together with land. In those cases the claim is not exclusively a land claim, yet it is still heilech because an effective lien remains. After clarifying the Rambam and the Rosh, we may examine the other authorities. Rashi explicitly explains the Gemara’s statement that “the document which he admits is heilech” by saying that this is because land is encumbered. The Giddulei Terumah cites this as proof, and the Shach in seif katan 47 attempts to reject it by saying that Rashi spoke only where the debtor does not admit the document. This is forced. Rashi is explaining the very phrase, “the document which he admits is heilech.” Since he does admit it, why should Rashi need to mention the land lien unless the lien is essential to the heilech rationale? Indeed, there is an additional difficulty for the Shach. Why did Rashi erase the older reading that explicitly says “since he admits it”? According to the Shach, Rashi could have retained it and explained that the Gemara’s initial assumption, before it concluded that there was a land lien, was that an ordinary document can be one without a property guarantee, as the Mishnah in Bava Metzia recognizes a document without such guarantee. Rashi could then have said that such a document is heilech only when the debtor admits it, precisely as the Shach maintains. Why did Rashi reject that reading? Necessarily, Rashi held that if there is no lien upon property, the admitted amount is not heilech in any form, because there is no assured source of collection. If there is a lien upon property, the creditor does not need the debtor’s admission. Rashi therefore removed the phrase “since he admits it.” This is clear support for the Giddulei Terumah. Still, one can distinguish Rashi’s view. Rashi elsewhere holds that even in an ordinary loan, if the defendant places the admitted money before beit din, that is not heilech. Only a deposit already in the claimant’s domain in a legal sense is heilech. According to Rashi, mere inability to deny certainly cannot be superior to physically placing money before beit din. He therefore had to explain that an existing lien upon property makes the sum as though already collected and continuously standing in the creditor’s possession, like a deposit. According to the halakhah, however, we do not follow Rashi on that point, and one could argue that whenever denial is impossible it is as though the defendant hands the money over before beit din, which would suffice for heilech. This somewhat weakens the proof from Rashi. Nevertheless, the overall argument remains compelling, and the Asufot Zekenim cites many authorities who expressly require not only inability to deny but also a lien upon land. One should therefore not depart from the Mechaber’s ruling, and he deserves praise for stating it as he did.

urim_vetumim_urim.he: אפילו יש בו נאמנות והש"ך חולק דכיון דאין יכול לכפור תו לא הוי הודאה ועיין תומים שהארכתי בביטול דבריו וכתבתי דרוב מחברים לא ס"ל כן:
urim_vetumim_urim.en: Even if it contains a credibility clause. Shach disagrees: if the debtor cannot deny the written obligation because of the credibility clause, then his admission should no longer count as a partial admission. See Tumim, where I refuted this at length and showed that most authorities do not accept Shach's position.

mechaber.he: ואם מסר לוה למלוה כתב ידו בפני עדים נתבאר בסימן (מ' וס"ט) שדינו כשטר שחתומים בו עדים:
mechaber.en: And if a message to Moses, he wrote to the witnesses, he would be found in the sign (M.S. and S.) that he discussed as he had witnessed:

baer_hetev.he: נתבאר. עיין לעיל ס"ס נ"א:
baer_hetev.en: We will be well. See the above paragraph:

siftei_kohen.he: נתבאר כו'. ועמ"ש בזה בס"ס נ"א:
siftei_kohen.en: We'll be well-known. This is the case at the SJ:

mechaber.he: תבעו מנה הלויתיך בניסן ומנה בתשרי והודה לו בא' מהם חשיב שפיר ממין הטענה אע"פ שלא הלוהו כאחד:
mechaber.en: If one claims, 'I lent you one hundred in Nisan and one hundred in Tishrei,' and the defendant admits one of the loans, the admission is properly regarded as being of the same kind as the claim even though the two loans were not made together.

beer_hagolah.he: טור סל"ב בשם בה"ת
beer_hagolah.en: The columnist named her

beur_hagra.he: תבעו מנה כו'. כן הוכיחו מדברי הרי"ף שכ' בסכ"ח שאין נשבע על הודאת השטר אע"ג שבלא"ה ב' ענינים הן מלוה בשטר ומלוה ע"פ ודברי רי"ף הן בירושלמי פ"ב דכתובות מודה חביבי בשטר היך עבידא טענו מנה וכפר בו והוציא שטר שחייב לו חמשין אין לו אלא חמשין ועמש"ל סי' ע"ה ס"ב:
beur_hagra.en: He claimed a maneh from him... This was inferred from the Rif's words in seif 28, where he says that no oath is imposed by an admission contained in a document, even though a loan in a document and an oral loan are otherwise two distinct categories. The Rif's source is the Yerushalmi, second chapter of Kesubos: "My uncle concedes regarding a document." How so? One claimed a maneh, the defendant denied it, and the claimant produced a document establishing fifty; he has only the fifty. See what I wrote above in siman 75 seif 2.

urim_vetumim_urim.he: אע"פ שלא הלוהו כאחד פי' ודאי תבעו בחיטין והודה לו בשעורים לא הוה דהא אין אדם תובע כל תביעתו כאחד אלא אפילו שבועה מחייב דה"א דאין הודאה ממין טענה קמ"ל דלא:
urim_vetumim_urim.en: A.A. who has not been identified as one of P.S. must have sued him and confessed to him in the shackles that he has not been given any claim as one, but even a oath that is required by Dalai Lamin

mechaber.he: שטר חוב שכתוב בו סלעים או דינרים סתם מלוה אומר חמש ולוה אומר שתים פטור משבועה דאורייתא שאין כאן הודאה דבלאו הודאתו מיעוט סלעים שנים ונמצא שלא הודה אלא מה שבשטר ואין כאן הודאה ואפי' אמר הלוה ג' שהודה לו באחד יתר על משמעות השטר אפ"ה פטור משום דהוי כמשיב אבידה דאם רצה היה אומר שנים לפיכך א"ל מנה לך או לאביך בידי ופרעתיך מחצה והשיב זה לא הייתי זכור אך אתה הזכרתני יודע אני שלא פרעת כלום פטור ואפי' משבועת היסת שאינו אלא כמשיב אבידה:
mechaber.en:
A debt that is written in it by rocks or mere dinars says five and no one says that you are exempted from a bubble that is not here the admission of Dovlo, who has given him a few rocks and that he has not confessed but what is wrong and there is no confession here, and that he has not been mentioned in any of the significance of the AHP because he is exempted as a return of his father if he had not known for years
